name: Jamal Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Jamal. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any AI company, employer, union, party or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential and your name won't be attached to it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for Northfield Homes, a housing co-op builder, so we put up affordable timber-frame houses for people on the waiting list. Half my week is in the yard shed nailing up wall panels on a bench, the other half is on site on the new estate off Mill Lane, standing the panels up and fixing roof trusses, the triangle frames that hold the roof. I like that the houses go to real families, I've met some of them. What wears me out is the panels being late from the yard and then us rushing in the rain.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's your life like outside work, and money?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I share a flat with my partner Leo, he's doing a nursing degree so money is tight, it's mostly my wage. Co-op pay is a bit lower than the big builders, and there aren't many timber-frame jobs near here anyway. We've got less than a month saved. I'm a bit of a gadget person, I use AI every day, for working out cut lists, asking about building codes, even planning our food shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Huh. Honestly, I'd be a bit disappointed. I was looking forward to some of the cool stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's still useful, it just isn't magic. I'd tell the lads it saved me twenty minutes a day on cut lists and that's not nothing. Online I'd probably argue with the people saying it was all a scam, because I use it every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my job's safe and my pay stays low, so nothing gets better or worse. I'd still want to move up, maybe into the yard running the panel saw, because that's where the skills are going anyway. AI not changing much doesn't change the fact that I want more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Northfield and keep using the tools. I'd ask the yard manager, Grace, if I could train on the big panel saw, the computer-controlled one that cuts the timber from a file. I'd keep pushing in the co-op meetings for a pay rise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit flat, like when a film everyone hyped turns out to be just okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd argue with people calling it a scam. What would you tell them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I measured a bathroom stud wall last week, typed the numbers in, and it gave me a cut list with the waste worked out. My foreman Pete does that on a scrap of plasterboard with a pencil and it takes him ten minutes. It's not magic, but it's real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does moving up mean for you, in money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a bit more an hour if I'm on the panel saw, and indoor work in winter. That's worth a lot to me. Leo finishes his degree in two years, and then we'd breathe.

S0.say: I'd say AI is still useful, just not magic, and that it saves me twenty minutes a day on cut lists. Online I'd argue with people calling it a scam, because I use it every day.
S0.think: Privately it means my job is safe and my pay stays low. I'd still want to move into the yard running the panel saw, because that's where the skills are going.
S0.do: Keeps working at Northfield Homes and keeps using AI tools. Asks the yard manager to train him on the computer-controlled panel saw and pushes for a pay rise at co-op meetings.
S0.feel: Calm, a little flat, like a hyped film that turned out just okay.
S0.quote: It's not magic, but it's real.
S0.fieldNote: Jamal is the rare worker slightly disappointed that AI fizzles. His ambition to move into the panel yard is independent of AI and comes from wanting better pay and indoor work. Money is tight because his partner is studying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now that's interesting. That's the one I actually think is coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a chance to make building better and safer, if workers get a say. In the co-op meetings I'd say we should be the ones choosing which machines come in, not some supplier. Online I'd post about the co-ops in other countries that share the gains with their workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd do well, if I move early. The panel yard is already half machines, and the people who can run them and fix them will be the ones kept. The ones I worry about are the older guys like Pete who won't touch a tablet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Grace to put me on the panel saw straight away and do the course the supplier runs. I'd look up a robotics or CNC course at the college, CNC is computer-controlled cutting, maybe evenings. I'd try to save a bit, but honestly the course money would come first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm. Excited, even, with a small knot about the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said course money comes first, even with less than a month saved. Isn't that risky?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, a bit. But if I sit still and save fifty a week, I've got a small pile and the same old job. If I spend it on a course, I've got a skill. I'd rather bet on me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Pete if the yard gets more machines?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd offer to show him, quietly, not in front of the lads. He taught me to frame a window when I was nineteen. I owe him that.

S1.say: I'd say it's a chance to make building better and safer if workers get a say, and that the co-op should choose which machines come in. Online I'd share examples of co-ops that share the gains with workers.
S1.think: Privately I think I'd do well if I move early, because the people who run and fix the yard machines will be the ones kept. I worry more for older colleagues like Pete.
S1.do: Asks to be put on the panel saw straight away and takes the supplier's course. Enrols in an evening CNC or robotics course at the college, paying for it before saving.
S1.feel: Calm and even excited, with a small knot of worry about money.
S1.quote: If I spend it on a course, I've got a skill. I'd rather bet on me.
S1.fieldNote: Jamal sees steady disruption as opportunity and would spend his thin savings on training rather than hold them. His progressive views come out as wanting workers to choose the machines. He shows loyalty to his older foreman Pete.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay. That's different. That's the robots running the panel saw too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to share this now, not later, and that the co-op model is the answer: workers owning the robots, not just companies. I'd go to every meeting and protest about it. I'd say it on social media every day, probably to the point of annoying people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think being good with tech doesn't save me if the machine is better than me at the tech too. My edge is being early, and in two years there is no early. And Leo would still be in his degree, so we'd have no second income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the co-op board to buy robots and keep us on as the people running them, with shorter hours and the same pay. I'd learn every new system that came in, the first day, so I'm the one they keep. I'd look for any job in installing or fixing site robots, even if it meant leaving Northfield, and I'd sign up for whatever support there was.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicking yet, but my chest is tight just thinking about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You talked about shorter hours with the same pay. Do you think a co-op could afford that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, honestly. If the robots build the house for less, the savings have to go somewhere. In a co-op at least we get a vote on where. In a normal firm, it'd just be the boss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car. We'd sell it and I'd cycle to the yard, it's only four miles. Then Leo's phone contract, he'd moan, and then my takeaway coffee, which sounds small but is like twenty a week.

S2.say: I'd say we need to share this now, and that workers owning the robots through co-ops is the answer. I'd go to every meeting and protest and post about it every day.
S2.think: Privately I think being good with tech doesn't help if the machine is better at the tech too. My edge is being early, and in two years there is no early.
S2.do: Pushes the co-op board to buy robots and keep workers on as operators with shorter hours and the same pay. Learns every new system on day one, looks for robot install or repair jobs elsewhere, and sells the car.
S2.feel: Anxious, with a tight chest, but not panicking yet.
S2.quote: My edge is being early, and in two years there is no early.
S2.fieldNote: Even for an adaptive person, two years removes his main advantage of moving first. He reaches for collective ownership through the co-op rather than personal escape alone. Money pressure is sharper because his partner has no income yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's enough time for Leo to finish and get a job. That changes a lot for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years to set this up right: a tax on robot use, worker ownership, training for everyone. I'd want the co-op to be an example. I'd tell everyone at the yard to learn the machines now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is enough for me to get properly good at something nearby, like programming and maintaining the panel machines. Leo would be working by then, and a nurse has more time than a carpenter in this picture, I think. So we'd have one steady wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the CNC course in the first year and then a robotics maintenance course, part-time. I'd save a bit each month once Leo's working, maybe aim for three months' money. And I'd try to get onto the co-op board, because I'd want to be in the room when they buy machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. There's a plan, and I like having a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a nurse has more time than a carpenter. Does it bother you that Leo might be safer than you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, if I'm honest. I've always been the one bringing the money in. But I'd rather one of us is safe than neither, and he'd do the same for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does five years feel better or worse than ten would, for someone your age?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better than two, obviously. But maybe five is the sweet spot for me, because it's long enough to train and short enough that I'd actually do it instead of putting it off.

S3.say: I'd say we've got five years to set this up right, with a tax on robot use, worker ownership and training for everyone. I'd want our co-op to be the example and tell everyone at the yard to learn the machines now.
S3.think: Privately five years is enough to get properly good at programming and maintaining the panel machines. By then Leo would be working as a nurse, so we'd have one steady wage.
S3.do: Takes a CNC course in the first year and then part-time robotics maintenance training. Saves towards three months of money once Leo is working and stands for the co-op board.
S3.feel: Uneasy but steadied by having a plan.
S3.quote: Maybe five is the sweet spot for me, because it's long enough to train and short enough that I'd actually do it instead of putting it off.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets Jamal line up his training with his partner finishing a degree. He admits, a little reluctantly, that Leo's nursing job may be safer than his own. Getting onto the co-op board is his way of shaping how machines arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. Funny, that's how old Pete was when he trained me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to do this fairly and there's no excuse if we don't. I'd be pushing the co-op and the union to plan the whole transition, training and pay for every worker. I'd probably be the annoying one at every meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years feels almost comfortable. I'd train, I'd move up, maybe run the machine side of the yard. My worry is the end point, when the machines can fix themselves too, and I genuinely don't know what I'd do then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd train in robotics maintenance over a few years, slowly. I'd try to start a little side thing teaching older tradespeople how to use the new tools, because I'm good at explaining and they'd need it. And I'd save, because with ten years and Leo working we could actually build a cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, not much more. Far enough away to plan around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd teach older tradespeople. Would people pay for that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe through the union or the college, not privately. Guys like Pete won't pay to learn a tablet, but they'd come if it was free and the coffee was good. I'd want to do it either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra time change compared with two years, in one sentence?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'm fighting to keep a job, with ten I'm choosing which job to have.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to do this fairly, so there's no excuse if we don't. I'd push the co-op and the union to plan the whole transition with training and pay for every worker.
S4.think: Privately ten years feels almost comfortable, long enough to train and run the machine side of the yard. My worry is the end point, when machines can fix themselves too, and I don't know what I'd do then.
S4.do: Trains in robotics maintenance over several years and starts a side line teaching older tradespeople to use new tools. Builds savings once Leo is working.
S4.feel: Mildly uneasy; it's far enough away to plan around.
S4.quote: With two years I'm fighting to keep a job, with ten I'm choosing which job to have.
S4.fieldNote: Jamal sees ten years as a real career runway, but is honest that the end point is still unknown to him. His side idea of teaching older tradespeople mirrors his loyalty to Pete. He wants the transition planned collectively, not left to the market.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there's no early in it, and early is the only thing I've got. What would help is the co-op owning the machines, so the savings come back to us, and free training that you can do while you're still working. Some kind of income floor, too, so nobody's choosing between a course and rent.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the houses. Northfield builds homes for people on a waiting list for years. If robots build them cheaper and faster, those families get homes sooner. I want that. I just want the people building them to get something too.

headlineQuote: If robots build them cheaper and faster, those families get homes sooner. I want that.
portrait: Jamal Jensen is a 27-year-old timber-frame carpenter at a housing co-op builder, splitting his week between the panel yard and the new estate, and supporting his partner Leo through a nursing degree on less than a month of savings. He uses AI every day and is a little disappointed by the plateau. He sees steady disruption as a chance to move into computer-controlled machines, gets anxious at AGI in two years because his edge of being early disappears, and feels more settled with five or ten years to train. Throughout, he wants workers to own the machines through the co-op.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because there is no time to be early, and being early is his only advantage.
whatWouldHelp: Co-op ownership of the machines so the savings come back to workers, free training he can do while working, and an income floor so nobody chooses between a course and rent.
